lesson.title: The Electrons That Stay Out of the Reaction
lesson.summary: Core electrons are the electrons in an atom's filled inner shells, everything that is not a valence electron, and they shield the nucleus's charge rather than participating directly in bonding.
lesson.body:
Every electron in an atom falls into one of exactly two categories: valence or core. You already know how to find valence electrons, the ones in the outermost occupied shell. Core electrons are simply everything else, the electrons packed into the complete, lower energy shells underneath the valence shell. Where valence electrons are the outward facing electrons that do the chemical work of bonding, core electrons sit close to the nucleus, tightly held, and under ordinary chemical conditions they do not get involved in forming or breaking bonds at all.

Finding the number of core electrons in a given atom is arithmetic once you already have the full electron configuration and the valence count: core electrons equal total electrons minus valence electrons. Take chlorine again, since you already worked out its full picture: 17 total electrons, configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5, and 7 valence electrons sitting in the n = 3 shell. That leaves 17 minus 7, or 10 core electrons, exactly the 2 electrons in 1s, 2 in 2s, and 6 in 2p that fill the n = 1 and n = 2 shells completely.

There is a pattern worth noticing here that will make noble gas notation, coming up next, feel obvious rather than arbitrary: for a main group element, the number of core electrons almost always equals the total electron count of the nearest preceding noble gas. Chlorine's 10 core electrons exactly match neon's 10 total electrons, because neon, atomic number 10, is the noble gas whose configuration (1s2 2s2 2p6) chlorine's inner shells duplicate precisely. This is true generally: whatever noble gas sits just before an element on the periodic table, that noble gas's full electron count is exactly the element's core electron count, since the noble gas represents the last shell that gets completely filled before the next element starts a new, outer shell.

Core electrons matter chemically even though they rarely participate directly in bonds, because they shield, or partially block, the full attractive pull of the nucleus from reaching the valence electrons. A valence electron does not feel the full positive charge of every proton in the nucleus; it feels a reduced, effective nuclear charge, because the core electrons sitting between it and the nucleus cancel out much of that pull. This shielding effect is a major reason atoms get larger as you move down a group (more filled inner shells means more shielding, so valence electrons sit farther out) and it helps explain trends in how tightly an atom holds onto its valence electrons.

The valence and core split is also exactly what makes noble gas notation possible as a writing shortcut. Since core electrons always mirror a noble gas's full configuration, chemists can replace that entire block of core electrons with the noble gas's symbol in brackets, writing out only the valence electrons explicitly. That shortcut, and the reasoning behind it, is the next concept.
